fields.expected: A few things about how I work that may be useful. I build systems around problems I actually run into, and I care a lot about where automation should stop. When I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript and Node, the interesting design question was not how autonomous I could make it but where machine action had to hand off to a person. I used SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, put every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED, and made free-text and demographic fields architecturally impossible to autofill. I also built a validation ladder (unit, fixture, live read-only, live mutation) so nothing gets called working just because it passes against a local fixture. Separately, I built and shipped an iOS health product, ClarityAtlas, into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, including a passive sleep-estimation system using HealthKit and Core Motion signals instead of a wearable. I am an undergraduate, not a senior engineer, but I have shipped things that real people used and found the failure modes.

fields.expected: The problem I would want to work on is deciding when an autonomous vessel's own output should be trusted, and what happens when it should not be. From what is public, Saronic builds autonomous surface vessels involving autonomy, sensor fusion, and real-time processing, and forward deployment means the system has to hold up in the field rather than in a test harness. That maps onto work I have already done. At Summer Atlantic Capital I built the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection system: temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer, because a detector that fires constantly creates a second problem instead of solving the first. I also built an explanation layer so an analyst could understand why something was flagged. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard to surface systematic failure modes. Generating an output is cheap; judging it is the hard part. On a vessel with degraded sensors and no operator nearby, I would want to work on detecting when perception is wrong and making that boundary explicit rather than silently absorbed.
